Content:
Suppose that we have the two functions [MATH: u(x)=2x^3] and [MATH: v(x)=x^2.] How do we calculate the derivative of their product [MATH: (u(x) \cdot v(x))'?]

Content:
To do that, we can use the product rule, which states that the derivative of the product of two functions is given by the formula
[MATH: \left(u(x) \cdot v(x)\right)' = u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x).]

Content:
In our case, the derivatives of the two functions are given by

Content:
[MATH: u^{′}(x)|= (2x^{3})^{′} = 6x^{2},; v^{′}(x)|= (x^{2})^{′} = 2x.]

Content:
If we plug all of this into the product rule formula, we get
[MATH: (u(x) ⋅ v(x))^{′}|= (6x^{2})(x^{2}) + (2x^{3})(2x); = 6x^{4} + 4x^{4}; = 10x^{4}.]

Content:
This example was quite simple, and we could have solved it by calculating the product first and then taking the derivative. We can do it now to double check our result:

Content:
[MATH: (u(x) ⋅ v(x))^{′}|= (2x^{3} ⋅ x^{2})^{′}; = (2x^{5})^{′}; = 10x^{4}✓]

Content:
Sometimes, however, we cannot calculate the product algebraically, or it can be tedious to do it. In those cases, the product rule will turn out to be very useful!

key_prerequisites.name: Calculating the Slope of a Tangent Line Using Differentiation

sections.normalized_html: If a curve [MATH: \mathcal C] is given by [MATH: y=e^x\sin x,] calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where [MATH: x=\dfrac \pi 2.]
sections.readable_text: If a curve [MATH: \mathcal C] is given by [MATH: y=e^x\sin x,] calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where [MATH: x=\dfrac \pi 2.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let [MATH: u(x) = e^x] and [MATH: v(x)=\sin{x}.] Then, we have

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = e^x,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x} = \cos x.]

Applying the product rule gives

[MATH: (dy)/(dx)|= u(dv)/(dx) + v(du)/(dx); = e^{x} ⋅ \cos x + \sin x ⋅ e^{x}; = e^{x}(\cos x + \sin x).]

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute [MATH: x=\dfrac\pi 2] into the formula and get

[MATH: (dy)/(dx)|_{x = π/2}|= e^{π/2}(\cos ((π)/(2)) + \sin ((π)/(2))); = e^{π/2}(0 + 1); = e^{π/2}.]

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is [MATH: e^{\pi/2}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that we have the two functions [MATH: u(x)=2x^3] and [MATH: v(x)=x^2.] How do we calculate the derivative of their product [MATH: (u(x) \cdot v(x))'?]

Content:
To do that, we can use the product rule, which states that the derivative of the product of two functions is given by the formula
[MATH: \left(u(x) \cdot v(x)\right)' = u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x).]

Content:
In our case, the derivatives of the two functions are given by

Content:
[MATH: u^{′}(x)|= (2x^{3})^{′} = 6x^{2},; v^{′}(x)|= (x^{2})^{′} = 2x.]

Content:
If we plug all of this into the product rule formula, we get
[MATH: (u(x) ⋅ v(x))^{′}|= (6x^{2})(x^{2}) + (2x^{3})(2x); = 6x^{4} + 4x^{4}; = 10x^{4}.]

Content:
This example was quite simple, and we could have solved it by calculating the product first and then taking the derivative. We can do it now to double check our result:

Content:
[MATH: (u(x) ⋅ v(x))^{′}|= (2x^{3} ⋅ x^{2})^{′}; = (2x^{5})^{′}; = 10x^{4}✓]

Content:
Sometimes, however, we cannot calculate the product algebraically, or it can be tedious to do it. In those cases, the product rule will turn out to be very useful!

---

[MATH: \eqalign{
(x\cos x)' &= u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x)\
&= (x)'\cdot \cos x + x\cdot (\cos x)'\
& = 1 \cdot \cos x + x (-\sin x)\
& = \cos x - x \sin x

}]

Example Prompt:
If a curve [MATH: \mathcal C] is given by [MATH: y=e^x\sin x,] calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where [MATH: x=\dfrac \pi 2.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let [MATH: u(x) = e^x] and [MATH: v(x)=\sin{x}.] Then, we have

[MATH: (dy)/(dx)|= u(dv)/(dx) + v(du)/(dx); = e^{x} ⋅ \cos x + \sin x ⋅ e^{x}; = e^{x}(\cos x + \sin x).]

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute [MATH: x=\dfrac\pi 2] into the formula and get

[MATH: (dy)/(dx)|_{x = π/2}|= e^{π/2}(\cos ((π)/(2)) + \sin ((π)/(2))); = e^{π/2}(0 + 1); = e^{π/2}.]

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is [MATH: e^{\pi/2}.]
